newsitem.title: FRANCE: Top French scientist resigns in gene maize row.
newsitem.headline: Top French scientist resigns in gene maize row.

text.p: A top scientist who led research for the French government into gene-modified maize resigned on Thursday to protest against a government decision to ban its production in France.

"The French government has banned sowings of a product it had itself promoted in Brussels. I cannot continue to work because my credibility with my European colleagues has been reduced to zero," Axel Kahn, head of the independent Biomolecular Genetics Commission (CGB), told Reuters.
Kahn's group had declared the maize safe and was at the forefront of French efforts to get the European Union to clear it. The EU's executive Commission agreed to do so in December.
In a move which also outraged French farmers, however, the government on Wednesday banned sowings of the maize for at least a year, saying it wanted to move step by step on a complex issue.
The decision came days after France also said it would allow imports of the maize, subject to labelling conditions.
"I think it was right for me to resign in view of the government's position," Kahn said in an interview.
Kahn said he believed the decision by the French cabinet was a political one and reflected pressure from consumers.
Environmentalists and some consumer groups have campaigned against the maize, saying it may damage to health. Kahn said there was no evidence of this.
"This is an issue where no scientist -- not even ecologist ones -- has been able to find the slightest risk," he said.

Pharmaceuticals giant Novartis AG, the merged successor to Swiss groups Ciba-Geigy, which invented the maize, and Sandoz, said on Thursday the French planting ban gave that country's farmers a competitive disadvantage.
It said it hoped the government would change its mind.
The gene-altered maize was designed to resist the corn (maize) borer pest. It has been approved in the EU, the U.S. and Canada.
